strengths: Principled and well-designed framework: Combining discrete flow matching on coarse fragment graphs with continuous flow matching over a latent connectivity vector and an exact maximum-weight matching reconstruction (via the Blossom algorithm) elegantly resolves the ambiguity and scalability issues of fragment-based molecular generation.

Effective stochastic fragment bag strategy: The use of an Info-NCE formulation to avoid computing expectations over an intractable fragment vocabulary enables the model to handle open and vast fragment spaces efficiently during both training and inference.

Comprehensive empirical validation: FragFM achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance across standard benchmarks (MOSES, GuacaMol) and significantly outperforms both atom-level and fragment-level baselines on the proposed NPGen benchmark, especially on functionality-driven metrics.

Remarkable sampling efficiency: FragFM maintains over 96% chemical validity and sub-1.0 FCD with as few as 10 to 50 denoising steps, drastically outperforming atom-level diffusion/flow models that suffer severe degradation at low step budgets.

Valuable benchmark contribution (NPGen): Introducing an open benchmark derived from COCONUT with biologically and chemically relevant evaluation metrics (NP-likeness, NP-Classifier taxonomies) addresses the saturation of MOSES/GuacaMol and provides substantial utility to the community.
weaknesses: Lower novelty and scaffold overlap on standard scaffold-split: On the MOSES benchmark using training fragments, FragFM achieves 87.1% novelty and 10.9% scaffold similarity (compared to ~95% novelty and 14-16% scaffold similarity for atom-based models). While supplying test-derived fragments improves the scaffold score to 24.5%, this reveals an inherent dependency of fragment-level generators on the coverage of the supplied fragment bag.

Missing direct quantitative comparison with recent fragment-based diffusion methods: Although the paper cites recent fragment-level diffusion works (such as Levy & Rector-Brooks and Chen et al.), empirical comparisons are restricted to autoregressive fragment models (JT-VAE, HierVAE) and atom-level diffusion/flow models.

Theoretical approximations in fragment-bag conditional guidance: The derivation for the guidance ratio in Appendix A.4 relies on a first-order Taylor expansion assumption that consecutive diffusion states evolve smoothly with negligible bag distribution divergence, which is heuristic and could benefit from further empirical ablation on varying step sizes $\Delta t$.

strengths: Sound and elegant formulation combining discrete flow matching over coarse fragment graphs with continuous flow matching over a latent vector that preserves fine-grained atomistic connectivity.

The stochastic fragment bag parameterization via Info-NCE loss effectively circumvents the vocabulary size bottleneck, enabling scalable training and generalizability across large, realistic fragment libraries.
Strong empirical results across standard benchmarks (MOSES, GuacaMol), showing exceptional chemical validity and state-of-the-art Fréchet ChemNet Distance (FCD) among one-shot generative models.

Remarkable sampling efficiency: FragFM maintains over 95% validity and competitive FCD with as few as 10 to 50 denoising steps, drastically outperforming atom-level diffusion models in fast-sampling regimes.
Introduction and curation of the NPGen benchmark derived from the COCONUT database, addressing the saturation and narrow domain of existing benchmarks with biologically relevant natural products.
Flexible property conditioning that leverages both standard classifier guidance on graph trajectories and property-biased fragment bag reweighting, achieving superior MAE-FCD trade-offs.
weaknesses: Under scaffold-split evaluation (MOSES), FragFM exhibits lower novelty (87.1%) and lower scaffold similarity (10.9%) when restricted to training-set fragments, highlighting an inherent constraint of fragment-based methods when novel scaffolds require unseen fragment combinations or unseen motifs.
The baseline evaluation on NPGen lacks recent continuous-time Markov chain or flow-matching baselines (e.g., Cometh, DeFoG), evaluating only DiGress among one-shot models.

A systematic ablation study on the sensitivity of the fragment bag size N during training and sampling, and its computational vs. distributional trade-off, would strengthen the methodological analysis.

strengths: Well-motivated architecture: Generating molecules at the fragment level significantly reduces the graph size and avoids the quadratic edge explosion and severe valency violations common in purely atom-based graph diffusion/flow models.

Sound hybrid formulation: Combining discrete flow matching (DFM) for categorical fragment nodes and edges with continuous flow matching (CFM) for the continuous autoencoder latent vector z provides an elegant, end-to-end framework. The coarse-to-fine autoencoder combined with the Blossom algorithm effectively resolves atomic connectivity ambiguity across fragment junctions.

Scalable fragment vocabulary handling: The stochastic fragment bag strategy trained via an Info-NCE objective bypasses the prohibitive expense of full-vocabulary softmax, enabling scalable training over large fragment libraries.

Strong generative fidelity and sampling efficiency: On standard benchmarks (MOSES and GuacaMol), FragFM achieves state-of-the-art FCD and validity among one-shot generative models, while retaining robust quality even down to 10–50 sampling steps.

Novel dual-level property conditioning: Combining classifier guidance with fragment bag reweighting (controlled by \lambda_B) allows fine-grained steering in chemical property and docking score spaces.
Introduction of NPGen: Curating and benchmarking on natural product structures from COCONUT provides a valuable, challenging benchmark that moves beyond saturated small-molecule benchmarks.
weaknesses: Lower novelty and scaffold diversity on standard splits: On MOSES (Table 1), FragFM shows noticeably lower novelty (87.1%) compared to atom-based models (>92%) and fragment autoregressive baselines (99.9%). The model's scaffold recovery is constrained by the fragment composition of the training bag.

Evaluation with test-set fragment bags: While evaluating with test-set fragments in Table 6 explains the scaffold drop, sampling test-set fragments during generation provides the model with prior knowledge about the test set, which cannot be directly compared to standard benchmark protocols.

Missing comparisons with recent multi-scale/fragment diffusion baselines: Although recent motif/fragment-based diffusion models (such as Levy & Rector-Brooks, 2023, or Chen et al., 2024) are cited in related work, empirical comparisons against them on MOSES or NPGen are missing.

Reliance on rigid fragmentation rules: The framework relies on BRICS decomposition rules, which may not decompose complex polycyclic or atypical natural product ring systems cleanly, potentially leaving large intact macrocycles as single fragments.
Unclear generation details for graph sizing: The main text leaves out how the initial coarse graph size (number of fragment nodes) is sampled prior to running the flow process.

strengths: Sound and innovative formulation: Combining discrete flow matching at the fragment level with continuous flow matching over a compact latent vector to recover fine-grained inter-fragment atomic connectivity (resolved globally via the Blossom algorithm) is elegant, technically sound, and addresses the notorious ambiguity problem in fragment assembly.

Effective stochastic fragment bag strategy: Addressing the vocabulary scaling bottleneck of fragment-based generation via InfoNCE training and an in-bag transition kernel is a clever solution that allows the framework to scale to tens/hundreds of thousands of fragments while keeping per-step computation bounded.

Introduction of the NPGen benchmark: Sourcing from COCONUT to benchmark larger, more structurally intricate natural-product molecules addresses an acknowledged issue of saturation and simplicity in standard benchmarks like MOSES and GuacaMol, providing valuable evaluation tools (NP-likeness KL, NPClassifier taxonomy) to the community.

Strong empirical performance and sampling efficiency: FragFM achieves state-of-the-art FCD and high validity across MOSES, GuacaMol, ZINC250k, and NPGen. In addition, it demonstrates remarkable robustness to reduced sampling step counts (e.g., 50 or even 10 steps), generating molecules much faster than standard atomistic discrete diffusion/flow baselines like DiGress.

Comprehensive experimental analysis: The manuscript includes thorough ablations and studies on the role of the latent vector $z$, fragment bag size, long-tail fragment recovery, temperature scaling for the fidelity-novelty trade-off, and the complementary effect of bag reweighting alongside classifier guidance.
weaknesses: Reliance on predefined fragmentation rules: FragFM relies on BRICS decomposition where cut sites are restricted to single bonds. This limits the flexibility of the decomposition on complex fused polycyclic systems that cannot be cleaved by BRICS without opening rings.

Trade-off on standard novelty and scaffold metrics: On the standard scaffold split of MOSES (Table 1), novelty (87.1%) and scaffold recovery (10.9) without test-bag supplementation are lower than those of purely atomistic models. While the authors adequately explain and provide temperature/test-bag remedies in the appendix, this inherent characteristic of fragment-based methods remains a practical trade-off.

Scope limited to 2D topological graph generation: While standard in 2D de novo graph generation benchmarks, the method does not model 3D conformations or structure-based pocket conditioning, which is increasingly relevant in practical computational drug design pipelines.

strengths: Well-motivated hierarchical formulation: Operating at the fragment level significantly reduces the graph size and avoids generating chemically invalid local atomic motifs, while the coarse-to-fine autoencoder with maximum-weight matching (Blossom algorithm) cleanly solves the ambiguity of fragment-to-atom reconstruction.

Clever and scalable training strategy: The stochastic fragment bag trained with an Info-NCE objective enables discrete flow matching over extensive, open fragment vocabularies without incurring computational costs that scale with the total vocabulary size.

Introduction of the NPGen benchmark: Providing a large-scale natural product generation benchmark derived from COCONUT addresses the saturation and narrow domain of existing small-molecule benchmarks (e.g., MOSES, GuacaMol) and incorporates domain-relevant metrics (NP-likeness, NPClassifier hierarchy).

Strong and thorough empirical validation: FragFM consistently achieves superior or competitive results across standard benchmarks and NPGen, demonstrating exceptional sampling efficiency (maintaining high validity and low FCD with as few as 10–50 steps) and effective dual-level conditional control via fragment bag re-weighting and classifier guidance.

Extensive analysis and ablation studies: The paper provides in-depth investigations into autoencoder reconstruction fidelity, long-tail fragment recovery, bag size sensitivity, temperature-controlled exploration, and qualitative samples.
weaknesses: Reliance on rigid fragmentation heuristics: Using BRICS rule-based fragmentation limits inter-fragment connections to predefined bond types (predominantly single bonds), which may restrict the model's ability to explore non-standard or unconventional chemical linkages outside BRICS rules.

Lower novelty on scaffold-constrained splits: On the MOSES scaffold split, the baseline FragFM achieves lower novelty and scaffold recovery unless test fragments or temperature scaling are incorporated, reflecting an inherent trade-off in fragment-based approaches.

Baseline scope on NPGen: While comparison against DiGress, GraphAF, JT-VAE, and HierVAE is informative, incorporating recent continuous/discrete flow baselines (e.g., DeFoG) or sequence-based fragment models (e.g., SAFE-GPT) on NPGen would make the benchmark evaluation even more comprehensive.

strengths: Principled and scalable framework: Combining discrete flow matching (DFM) at the fragment level with continuous flow matching (CFM) for fine-grained connectivity latents, followed by maximum-weight matching via the Blossom algorithm, provides an elegant and mathematically sound solution to the atom-level scalability and validity bottlenecks of graph diffusion/flow models.

Stochastic fragment bag with Info-NCE: Real-world chemical spaces involve tens or hundreds of thousands of fragments. The proposed stochastic bag strategy with an Info-NCE density-ratio formulation neatly bypasses the need for restricted, fixed fragment vocabularies while keeping per-step CTMC updates computationally tractable.

Introduction of the NPGen benchmark: NPGen offers a valuable contribution to the molecular generative modeling community by shifting focus from saturated benchmarks (MOSES, GuacaMol) of small drug-like molecules to larger, structurally complex, and biologically relevant natural products, complete with domain-informed evaluation metrics (NP-likeness and NPClassifier KL divergences).

Strong empirical performance and sampling efficiency: FragFM achieves state-of-the-art FCD on multiple benchmarks while maintaining near-perfect validity without explicit post-hoc filtering. Moreover, FragFM exhibits remarkable robustness to reduced denoising steps (achieving strong fidelity with as few as 10–50 steps) and yields significant wall-clock speedups over atom-level diffusion models.

Dual-control conditional generation: The integration of fragment-bag conditioning (steering candidate pool selection via property re-weighting) with standard classifier guidance offers fine-grained and robust controllability, especially in extreme property regimes such as tight protein docking scores.

Extensive analysis and ablation: The appendix provides comprehensive validation, including coarse-to-fine autoencoder fidelity, the necessity of the latent vector z, long-tail fragment recovery, training/inference bag size ablations, and temperature-controlled novelty exploration.
weaknesses: Novelty and scaffold diversity trade-offs: On the standard MOSES benchmark, FragFM demonstrates lower novelty (87.1% vs. >92% for atom-based models) and scaffold similarity when restricted to training fragments, which is a known characteristic of fragment-based methods that assemble predefined motifs. While temperature scaling and test-fragment sampling mitigate this, further discussion on balancing motif preservation with creative exploration is warranted.

Lack of synthetic accessibility evaluation: The paper argues that natural products are biologically validated templates for drug design, but many complex natural product-like structures assembled from fragments can be synthetically intractable. Incorporating retrosynthetic accessibility metrics (e.g., SAscore, SYBA, or retrosynthetic search algorithms like AiZynthFinder) would provide stronger validation of practical utility.

Baseline coverage on NPGen: While FragFM is benchmarked against GraphAF, JT-VAE, HierVAE, and DiGress on NPGen, other recent discrete graph diffusion/flow architectures (e.g., DeFoG, Cometh) are absent from the NPGen evaluation table, likely due to computational cost on large molecules.

strengths: Well-motivated hierarchical generative framework: Moving graph flow matching from the atom level to chemically valid fragments directly addresses fundamental bottlenecks of atomistic graph generative models, including edge-sparsity scaling, ring strain, and chemical validity.

Technically sound formulation: The combination of discrete flow matching over a dynamically sampled fragment bag via Info-NCE loss, continuous flow matching on the latent connectivity variable z, and exact bipartite matching via the Blossom algorithm provides an elegant solution to the large-vocabulary and junction-ambiguity problems in fragment assembly.

Valuable benchmark contribution (NPGen): The introduction of NPGen based on COCONUT provides a timely and challenging benchmark that moves beyond saturated, small-molecule datasets (MOSES/GuacaMol) into complex, natural-product-like chemical spaces where topological diversity is crucial.

Comprehensive empirical validation: FragFM achieves state-of-the-art FCD, validity, and structural metrics across MOSES, GuacaMol, ZINC250k, and NPGen, while demonstrating substantial sampling speedups (e.g., 5x faster than DiGress on NPGen) and remarkable resilience at low step regimes (10–50 steps).

Novel dual-guidance strategy: Combining classifier guidance with fragment-bag probability re-weighting offers an intuitive and highly effective mechanism for conditional property steering without requiring end-to-end model retraining.

Thorough ablations and chemistry-grounded analysis: The retrosynthetic feasibility study (AiZynthFinder), ablation of the latent code z and Blossom decoder, analysis of rare-fragment recovery, and sensitivity to bag sizes and fragmentation rules (BRICS, RECAP, rBRICS) provide strong support for the claims.
weaknesses: Lower scaffold recovery on scaffold-split benchmarks: On the MOSES scaffold-split test, FragFM obtains lower scaffold overlap and novelty than some atomistic baselines. While Section C.4 demonstrates that providing test-set fragment vocabularies resolves this, evaluating with test-set fragments is unconventional in standard benchmark settings.

Comparison with sequence-based fragment models: In Table 2 (NPGen), the 1D sequence-based SAFE-GPT achieves noticeably better FCD and KL divergence than FragFM, albeit with reduced novelty (73.5% vs 95.4%). The manuscript would benefit from a deeper qualitative and quantitative discussion contrasting the inductive biases and practical tradeoffs of sequence-based fragment approaches versus graph-based fragment approaches.

Graph size specification during sampling: The generation process outlines how node types, edges, and latent vectors are sampled, but the description of how the initial coarse graph size (number of fragment nodes) is sampled or determined during unconditional and conditional inference should be made clearer in the main text.

strengths: Principled and elegant formulation: Combining discrete flow matching (DFM) at the fragment level with a continuous-time Markov chain trained via an Info-NCE objective over stochastic fragment bags neatly addresses the vocabulary explosion bottleneck inherent to fragment-based generative modeling.

Effective lossless hierarchical reconstruction: The coarse-to-fine autoencoder pairing continuous latent flow matching with the Blossom algorithm achieves >99% bond-level reconstruction accuracy, resolving the ambiguity in junction-atom connectivity between fragments.

Introduction of the NPGen benchmark: Introducing a curated, large-scale natural product benchmark (COCONUT-derived) fills an important gap in the community, providing a domain-specific stress test where conventional atom-based models struggle due to complex ring topologies and high heteroatom densities.

Comprehensive experimental validation and efficiency: FragFM significantly outperforms prior graph generative models on standard benchmarks (MOSES, GuacaMol, ZINC250k) and NPGen in terms of validity, FCD, and physical plausibility, while providing up to a 5x speedup in sampling time and notable robustness under few denoising steps (e.g., 10–50 steps).

Novel dual-guidance capability: The combination of standard classifier guidance with property-conditioned fragment bag reweighting offers a unique, flexible control knob for goal-directed generation without retraining the core generative model.
weaknesses: Scaffold diversity under strict splits: On scaffold-split benchmarks (like MOSES), generating unseen scaffolds is intrinsically limited when sampling strictly from training-set fragments, leading to lower Scaf and novelty metrics compared to purely atomistic baselines unless temperature scaling or test fragment vocabularies are applied.

Comparison with sequence-based models: On the NPGen benchmark, sequence-based SAFE-GPT achieves substantially lower FCD and distribution KL divergences than FragFM (albeit at lower novelty). A deeper discussion on the trade-offs between fragment graph flows and autoregressive string models would further contextualize these results.

Reliance on rule-based fragmentation heuristics: Although the authors show robustness across BRICS, RECAP, and rBRICS, the framework still fundamentally depends on pre-defined chemical cleavage rules, which may constrain bond formation to predefined junction types.

strengths: Principled and well-engineered framework: FragFM addresses the computational and structural challenges of atom-based diffusion/flow models by operating at the fragment level with discrete flow matching, coupled with a coarse-to-fine autoencoder and the Blossom algorithm to recover atom-level connectivity with over 99% accuracy.

Scalable handling of large fragment vocabularies: The stochastic fragment bag strategy combined with an Info-NCE density-ratio formulation elegantly bypasses the prohibitive cost of evaluating rate matrices over vast chemical fragment libraries.

Dual-level controllable generation: The paper introduces a synergistic conditioning framework that combines target-guided fragment bag selection with state-level classifier guidance, demonstrating superior property steering (e.g., JAK2 docking scores, ring counts, QED) without catastrophic drops in molecular validity.

Introduction of the NPGen benchmark: Proposing a large-scale natural product benchmark curated from COCONUT provides a much-needed, realistic stress test for generative models beyond saturated benchmarks like MOSES and GuacaMol.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Extensive experiments across multiple datasets (MOSES, GuacaMol, ZINC250k, NPGen), ablations on fragmentation rules (BRICS, RECAP, rBRICS), bag sizes, latent representations, retrosynthetic accessibility (AiZynthFinder), and long-tail fragment recovery thoroughly support the claims.
Sampling efficiency: FragFM retains high validity (>96%) and low FCD even with as few as 10 to 50 denoising steps, yielding notable wall-clock speedups over atom-level diffusion baselines.
weaknesses: Scaffold generalization under scaffold-split: On the MOSES scaffold-split test set, FragFM exhibits lower scaffold similarity (Scaf: 10.9) and slightly lower novelty compared to some atom-based baselines. While Section C.4 demonstrates that supplying test-set fragments improves Scaf to 24.5, conditioning on test fragments relaxes the standard out-of-distribution evaluation protocol.

Pipeline complexity: The architecture consists of multiple distinct components (the fragment-to-vector MPNN, the coarse-to-fine latent autoencoder, discrete flow matching for nodes/edges, continuous flow matching for latent $z$, and the Blossom matching algorithm), which increases system complexity compared to end-to-end atomistic models.

Gap with autoregressive sequence baselines on distributional metrics: While FragFM substantially outperforms other graph-based models on NPGen, sequence-based SAFE-GPT achieves lower FCD and NP-score KL divergences (albeit at the expense of significantly lower novelty, 73.5% vs. 95.4%).
